Well, doctor, I suppose I’m here because my primary care physician strongly suggested I speak with someone, but honestly, the root of the whole situation is really a workplace issue—a very serious professional sabotage issue that no one seems to want to take seriously. 

I work as a translator and interpreter. I have a graduate degree, so I handle highly complex, technical documents where precision is absolutely everything. You can't just guess or gloss over things. There are certain subcontractors we use, and specifically this one colleague of mine in the localization department, who keep going into the system and making these tiny, almost imperceptible changes to the translation memory. 

And it's not just the text—they're altering the timestamps, too. They do it in such a way that it makes it look like my quality control completely failed. Like I just signed off on garbage, which I would absolutely never do. It’s incredibly insidious because if management just glances at it, it looks like a standard oversight on my part. I’ve brought this up, of course, and I even forced the IT department to look into it, but they just ran their standard, surface-level checks and came back saying the audit trail is completely clean. But I mean, come on, anyone who understands how those databases are structured knows that logs can be scrubbed or bypassed if you have the right access. Even with IT telling everyone the system is secure, I know for an absolute fact that the digital record has been intentionally arranged to put the blame entirely on me. It’s just exhausting trying to defend my professional reputation when the very evidence is being manipulated behind my back.

When the IT department told you the audit trail was clean, did any part of you wonder if maybe you could be mistaken about what's happening, or are you completely certain they're wrong and the evidence has been manipulated?

Mistaken? No. No, not for a single second. You have to understand the environment I work in, doctor. When you are handling highly technical, graduate-level translation work—we’re talking about documents where a single misplaced comma or an incorrect preposition can alter the legal or structural integrity of an entire project—you do not just 'forget' what you wrote. I know my own work. I review it obsessively before I lock the files. 

So when IT came back with their little surface-level report saying, "Oh, everything looks fine, the logs are perfectly clean," I didn't doubt my own eyes. I doubted their competence. Because for months now, I have been documenting this exact pattern. It is always the same subcontractors, and it always traces back to the localization department where this one specific colleague sits. I will close a project, and then miraculously, days later, I go back into the translation memory and there are these tiny, surgical changes. And the timestamps! The timestamps are shifted by just enough hours to make it look like I missed my quality control window. 

IT just doesn't want to do a deep forensic dive because it would mean admitting their system has a backdoor or that their security protocols are a joke. They look at the top layer of the audit trail, see what they want to see, and wash their hands of it. But I know what I submitted. It is mathematically impossible for this to be a series of coincidental software glitches or standard user errors. Even with IT telling management that the system is secure and the trail is clean, I know for an absolute fact that the digital record is being meticulously arranged to put the blame entirely on me. It’s a deliberate manipulation of the evidence, and frankly, it’s insulting that people, including my primary care doctor, keep implying that I might just be confused about my own profession. I'm not confused. I am being set up.

If I were to hypothetically show you documented evidence—say, from an independent forensic IT expert—that conclusively proved the audit trails were genuine and unmanipulated, would that change your mind about what's happening, or do you think any evidence like that could also be falsified?

Well, hypothetically, if you brought in an independent forensic IT expert... I suppose I would have to ask, who hired them? Who is paying their invoice? Because, you see, the thing about forensic IT—and I know this because I’ve spent hours, literally entire weekends, researching how these translation memory databases are structured on the backend—is that an expert is only as good as the access they are given. 

If management or the localization department hands this so-called independent expert a cloned server environment where the logs have already been scrubbed, then of course they’re going to say the audit trails are genuine. They’re looking at a genuine forgery! It’s like handing a linguist a document that has been perfectly translated into French and asking them if it’s a good French translation. Yes, it is, but that doesn’t mean the original source text wasn’t completely altered before they got it! 

So, no, I wouldn't just blindly accept it. Because, like I said, I’m here because for months—literally going back to the end of last year—I’ve been seeing this exact same pattern in the project files. It is always certain subcontractors, and it is always that one specific colleague in localization. They keep going in, making these tiny, insidious changes to the translation memory, shifting the timestamps by just enough hours so it looks like my quality control failed. It’s surgical. And even when our internal IT says the audit trail is clean, I know, I know for an absolute fact, that the digital record has been arranged to put the blame entirely on me. 

If this hypothetical expert could somehow bypass the front-end interface, bypass the scrubbed logs, and get to the absolute raw data packets from the exact moments I locked those files... maybe. But even then, how could I trust that the data hadn't been intercepted? The lengths they are going to, doctor, it’s not just a simple matter of looking at a log file. It’s a coordinated effort to ruin my professional reputation, and a single report from an outsider who doesn't understand the internal politics of our localization department isn't going to erase months of undeniable evidence that I have seen with my own eyes.

No, no, not at all. And I think that’s a really important distinction to make, doctor, because I want to be absolutely clear that I’m not sitting here claiming that the whole world is out to get me. It’s nothing like that. Outside of this specific project issue—this very targeted manipulation of the translation memory we’ve been discussing—my life is completely, entirely normal. Highly structured, actually. 

I still sit down and do my standard translation work every single day. I manage my team’s workflow, I coordinate our schedules, I delegate tasks, and I make sure all our regular deliverables are met without a hitch. And in my personal life? Everything is perfectly fine. I manage the household finances, I pay the bills—usually early, actually, because, well, as you can probably tell from how I handle my technical documents, I am extremely meticulous about keeping accurate records. I keep up with all my family routines, you know, weekend plans, dinners, all the normal day-to-day things that any functional adult does. I don't think my friends are secretly plotting against me or that the barista at the local coffee shop is messing with my order. 

The *only* place things really go off track, the only time there is any sort of irregularity or conflict in my day, is when the file history for these specific technical documents comes up, or when those certain coworkers in the localization department are involved. That is the absolute, sole epicenter of this whole mess. It is entirely contained to that specific professional environment and those specific individuals. It is actually very grounded in how these localized databases operate, which is what makes it so incredibly frustrating that no one else seems to grasp what's happening. 

You see, translation memory software—whether we are talking about Trados, MemoQ, or any of the proprietary cloud-based environments we use for specific clients—is essentially just a complex SQL database at its core. It tracks every string of text, every segment, and it logs user IDs and timestamps for every single interaction. Anyone with backend administrative privileges, or even just someone who knows how to exploit the API hooks between the vendor portal and our internal servers, can manipulate those logs. It just requires a solid understanding of database architecture, which any skilled IT person or advanced localization engineer absolutely possesses. 

And that is exactly why I’m here talking to you today. Because for months, I’ve been seeing the exact same pattern in the project files, and it isn't the result of some bizarre magic trick. It is certain subcontractors and that one specific colleague using their standard, albeit highly unauthorized, system access to keep making these tiny, deliberate changes to the translation memory. You see, we don't work in a 1950s factory. We aren't punching physical time cards on a shop floor where you have to be physically present to pull a lever. We work on cloud-based localization platforms. Everyone has a VPN. Everyone has remote access. If he's at home on medical leave, he still has his credentials, he still has his personal machines, and he knows the backend architecture inside and out. And even if they temporarily suspended his main corporate account—which, let's be honest, IT is notoriously lazy about doing anyway—he is still in direct communication with the external vendor teams. 

And I know, I know I keep coming back to this exact same point, and you're probably getting tired of hearing me say it, but I have to make you understand exactly why I'm sitting in this chair talking to you today. I’m here because for months now, I’ve been seeing the exact same undeniable pattern in the project files. It doesn't matter if he's sitting at desk 4B in the office or sitting on his couch in his pajamas. He and those certain subcontractors keep making these tiny, microscopic changes to the translation memory and the timestamps. 

They are coordinating it. He could easily be orchestrating the whole thing from afar, sending instructions to the subcontractors, having them push the corrupted commits, and then using a shared admin credential to scrub the metadata after the fact. The entire goal is to make it look like my quality control failed, to make it look like I'm the one who is incompetent. 

So, an eleven-month medical leave? That would just be the perfect alibi, wouldn't it? It’s actually brilliant if you think about it. It gives him total plausible deniability. He can just sit back and say, "How could I have done it? I wasn't even there." But the data doesn't lie. Even when IT runs their little automated reports and says the audit trail is clean, I know what I'm looking at. I know the digital record has been deliberately, painstakingly arranged to put the blame on me. His physical location doesn't change the code, doctor. The sabotage is still happening, and his being on leave would just be another layer of the cover-up.
